docs.title: iVedha Managed Elasticsearch Platform
docs.text:
The platform runs in the customer's Azure subscription. iVedha/Opsflw manages platform deployment and operations.

The iVedha Managed Elasticsearch Platform deploys Elasticsearch and Kibana on Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) through Azure Marketplace. It gives teams a managed foundation for search, observability, analytics, and eligible AI use cases without requiring them to build and operate the underlying Azure and Elastic platform alone.

The customer owns the Azure subscription, connectivity, identity, DNS, and data onboarding. iVedha operates the supported platform through Opsflw automation and managed interfaces.

docs.title: What the platform is
docs.text:
Azure Managed Applications creates a customer-visible application resource and a managed resource group for the platform infrastructure. Elasticsearch and Kibana run on AKS inside the customer's Azure subscription. Supporting services provide approved networking, identity, certificate, storage, monitoring, deployment, and lifecycle capabilities.

This is not Elastic Cloud hosted outside the customer environment, and it is not an unmanaged Kubernetes package. Customers use the Azure managed application, Elasticsearch, Kibana, and documented customer actions. They must not modify resources in the managed resource group unless a supported action explicitly permits the change.

The exact capacity, topology, endpoints, services, and licensed features depend on the approved Marketplace plan and deployed platform version.

docs.title: What you can use it for
docs.text: Workload Typical outcome Search Index and query application, product, knowledge, vector, or other document collections Observability Collect and analyze logs, metrics, traces, and operational events Analytics Explore indexed operational or business data in Elasticsearch and Kibana Eligible AI use cases Apply supported vector, inference, machine-learning, or AI-assisted features after version, license, capacity, and governance checks

docs.title: Who manages what
docs.text:
Party Primary responsibilities Customer Own the Azure subscription, billing, policy, quota, network routes, DNS, Microsoft Entra identity, Elastic license, data onboarding, retention, and workload outcomes iVedha Provide managed-service support and perform the platform administration, monitoring, maintenance, upgrades, and troubleshooting included in the approved service Opsflw Supply the automation that provisions, configures, reconciles, monitors, and performs supported lifecycle actions for the platform Microsoft Operate Azure and enforce Azure Marketplace and Azure Managed Application controls Elastic Define Elasticsearch and Kibana product behavior, compatibility, and license-based features

For task-level ownership and safety boundaries, see shared responsibility.

docs.title: Choose public or private connectivity
docs.text:
Both access models use service hostnames, TLS, authentication, and authorization.

  • Public connectivity exposes internet-reachable service endpoints. The customer must approve exposure, own the required public DNS, and apply the deployment-supported access restrictions.
  • Private connectivity uses an Azure Private Endpoint and a customer network route. The customer owns the Private Endpoint, private DNS path, and certificate-authority trust where a customer certificate is required.

Choose the model before deployment. Review the decision in plan connectivity.

docs.title: What Opsflw automation does
docs.text:
Opsflw automation coordinates the supported lifecycle of the managed application. It validates deployment inputs, provisions and configures the platform, reconciles the desired state, publishes customer-facing deployment details, monitors platform health, and runs supported maintenance and lifecycle actions.

Automation does not transfer ownership of the customer's subscription, identities, network, DNS, or data. A feature represented in automation is available to a customer only when the deployed plan and managed application expose it.

docs.title: What AI-ready means
docs.text:
AI-ready means the platform can provide the Elasticsearch and Kibana foundation for eligible full-text search, vector search, inference, and machine-learning use cases. It does not mean every AI model, Elastic feature, or external model service is automatically enabled.

Before adopting an AI use case, verify the deployed Elastic version and license, selected topology, optional machine-learning capacity, supported integration, outbound connectivity, credential ownership, and data-governance approval. Treat an unverified feature as unavailable.

docs.title: Follow the customer journey
docs.text:
1. Plan. Decide the Azure subscription, workload capacity, topology, connectivity, DNS, TLS, maintenance window, and owners.
  2. Deploy. Create the managed application from the approved Azure Marketplace offer and monitor every readiness gate.
  3. Complete Next Steps. Reset the administrator password, configure the selected network, DNS, and TLS path, and verify Elasticsearch and Kibana.
  4. Operate. Establish least-privilege access, onboard data, use the platform, and perform supported lifecycle tasks.
  5. Get Help. Diagnose the failing layer, collect safe evidence, and contact support through the managed application when needed.
  6. Use Reference. Look up architecture, responsibilities, lifecycle states, permissions, compatibility, limits, and terminology.

Start with the planning overview. For another iVedha application, return to the Opsflw documentation catalog.

docs.title: Limits rule
docs.text: Use limits shown by the approved Marketplace plan, Azure subscription quota, deployed resource configuration, and current Elastic version. Do not copy fixed capacity, retention, availability, or timing values from another deployment.

docs.title: Deployment checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Microsoft Entra tenant is recorded.
  • [ ] Azure subscription, region, quota, policy, and RBAC are approved.
  • [ ] Managed application name follows the customer naming policy.
  • [ ] Workload profile is selected from the approved Marketplace plan.
  • [ ] Capacity is supported by ingestion, retention, and query evidence.
  • [ ] Topology meets the availability and data-tiering requirements.
  • [ ] Public or private connectivity is approved.
  • [ ] DNS zone and record ownership are assigned.
  • [ ] Certificate or certificate-authority ownership is assigned.
  • [ ] Maintenance window and time zone are approved.
  • [ ] Operational and support contacts are recorded.
  • [ ] Marketplace purchase and selected plan are approved.

docs.title: Handover
docs.text:
• [ ] Azure and service readiness are successful.
  • [ ] Authoritative endpoints and resource IDs are recorded.
  • [ ] DNS, TLS, authentication, and least-privilege access are tested.
  • [ ] Synthetic ingestion and search are successful.
  • [ ] Monitoring, snapshots, and support routes are verified.
  • [ ] No secrets are present in handover records.

docs.title: Before a change
docs.text:
• [ ] Scope, owner, risk, validation, and rollback are approved.
  • [ ] Health and capacity are acceptable.
  • [ ] A usable snapshot is verified when required.
  • [ ] Affected users and clients are notified.

docs.title: Before deletion
docs.text:
• [ ] Data and recovery approvals are complete.
  • [ ] Ingestion is stopped or redirected.
  • [ ] Required exports and final snapshot are verified.
  • [ ] Dependent DNS, Private Endpoints, identities, and alerts are inventoried.

docs.title: Architecture details
docs.text: The platform combines Elastic Stack services with Azure infrastructure managed through an Azure Managed Application.

docs.title: Architecture overview
docs.text:
The managed platform runs in the customer's Azure subscription. Customers own the subscription, connectivity, identity, and data. A monitoring agent in the managed resource group forwards platform telemetry to the iVedha monitoring cluster so managed operations can observe platform health and respond to supported incidents.

The diagram is conceptual. The exact Azure resources depend on the approved offer, plan, region, and version. It intentionally omits subnets, node pools, node roles, and internal automation.

docs.title: Service components
docs.text:
• Elasticsearch stores, indexes, and searches data.
  • Kibana provides the browser interface for search, visualizations, dashboards, and supported administration.
  • Azure Kubernetes Service hosts the managed application workloads.
  • Azure Key Vault holds deployment secrets and certificate material.
  • Azure Storage supports deployment data, diagnostics, and snapshot access where configured.
  • Monitoring agent collects managed-resource platform telemetry and forwards it to the iVedha monitoring cluster.
  • Azure networking supplies virtual networks, private connectivity, DNS, and optional public access.
  • Managed identities and Azure RBAC authorize supported communication without embedding Azure credentials in documentation.

Not every underlying resource is intended for direct customer administration. Use the managed application view and documented Elasticsearch or Kibana interfaces for supported changes.

For component purpose, availability, placement, and ownership, see the platform component catalog.

docs.title: Managed monitoring flow
docs.text:
The monitoring agent runs in the managed resource group and forwards operational platform telemetry to the iVedha monitoring cluster outside the customer subscription. iVedha managed operations use the resulting health signals and alerts to investigate the supported platform.

This path represents platform monitoring. It does not mean that the customer's Elasticsearch indices or application data are hosted in the iVedha operations environment. Customers remain responsible for monitoring workload outcomes, data quality, ingestion behavior, and application-level service objectives.

docs.title: Azure resource boundaries
docs.text: Boundary Primary purpose Customer action Application resource group Contains the managed application instance View status and perform supported lifecycle actions Managed resource group Contains supporting infrastructure Inspect only as permitted; do not modify directly Customer network and DNS Connects users and data sources Configure approved routing, DNS, and Private Endpoints Elasticsearch data plane Holds customer indices and configuration Manage data, users, roles, and application-level settings

docs.title: Access models
docs.text:
Private access keeps service endpoints on approved private network paths. Users need a Private Endpoint, working DNS, a trusted TLS certificate, and a route from their client network.

Public access uses internet-reachable endpoints. It still requires TLS, authentication, and any organization-approved network restrictions.

Choose the access model during planning. Changing it later may require DNS, certificate, firewall, and client reconfiguration.

For a focused comparison, see plan connectivity.

docs.title: Renew TLS certificates
docs.text: Renew certificates before their validity period ends. Keep the old certificate available for controlled rollback until the new certificate is verified.

docs.title: Renew a private certificate
docs.text:
1. Inventory every service hostname and current expiration date.
  2. Generate a new private-scope CSR through the managed application action.
  3. Verify its subject alternative names.
  4. Have the approved certificate authority sign the CSR.
  5. Upload the public leaf and required intermediate certificate chain.
  6. Wait for the managed action to complete.

  7. From each client network, set the exact deployment-provided hostname and verify hostname, chain, and expiration:

    SERVICE_HOSTNAME="<deployment-service-hostname>"

openssl s_client \
  -connect "${SERVICE_HOSTNAME}:443" \
  -servername "${SERVICE_HOSTNAME}" \
  -verify_return_error </dev/null

  8. Confirm the command ends with Verify return code: 0 (ok) and the served certificate has the expected subject alternative name, issuer, serial number, and new expiration date.

  9. Test Kibana sign-in and an Elasticsearch request.
  10. Record the new expiration date and next renewal owner.

Do not upload or distribute the deployment private key. If the certificate is rejected, confirm that it was issued from the current CSR and that the complete chain is present. If clients still receive the old certificate, confirm that the managed action completed and retry from every endpoint and network path before assuming the change propagated.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: The deployed managed application is authoritative for its platform and Elastic versions. Do not select a client, Agent, integration, or feature from the documentation site's publication date.

docs.title: Record the deployment baseline
docs.text: Surface Authoritative location Required check Managed platform Managed application outputs or deployment details Record the platform version exposed by the deployment Elasticsearch GET / or an approved Kibana view Record the exact Elasticsearch version Kibana Kibana help or status view Confirm it matches the managed stack Elastic Agent and Fleet Fleet compatibility guidance for the deployed stack Confirm both the Agent and integration package versions OpenTelemetry Elasticsearch and Collector documentation for the deployed versions Confirm OTLP protocol, paths, exporter, and semantic-convention behavior Azure region and plan Approved Marketplace offer Confirm the selected plan is available in the deployment region Elastic license Kibana license view or supported managed action Confirm that every required feature is entitled

docs.title: Apply the compatibility rule
docs.text:
Before enabling a feature or changing a component:

  1. record the exact deployed versions;
  2. read the corresponding Elastic compatibility and upgrade guidance;
  3. confirm the feature is exposed by the managed application;
  4. test the change with representative non-production data;
  5. record rollback and support ownership.

The documentation intentionally does not publish an unverified global version matrix. A platform release must add its approved version range here before the release is described as supported.

See release notes for documentation changes and prepare for upgrades for managed upgrade planning.

docs.title: Choose a data onboarding path
docs.text:
Choose an ingestion path only after confirming that its endpoint and component are exposed by your deployment. A URL in source code is not proof that the corresponding service is enabled in your Marketplace plan.

Customers operate the source applications and collection layer. The managed platform receives approved TLS-protected ingestion traffic.

docs.title: Compare onboarding paths
docs.text: Source Starting path Verify before production Application telemetry OpenTelemetry Collector in gateway mode Elastic version, OTLP support, API-key privileges, TLS, batching, and back pressure Servers and virtual machines Elastic Agent managed by Fleet Fleet and Fleet Server endpoints, supported Agent version, egress, certificate trust, and policy ownership Kubernetes OpenTelemetry Collector or Elastic Agent DaemonSet or gateway design, namespaces, metadata policy, network egress, and resource limits Application search documents Elasticsearch API and a data stream or index mapping, template, API-key scope, document identity, lifecycle, and retry behavior Existing pipelines Logstash exposed endpoint, plugin versions, persistent queue, TLS, and credential rotation Azure services Verified Elastic integration or Event Hubs path service-specific integration, Event Hubs permissions, checkpointing, and cost Network and appliance logs Elastic Agent integration or controlled syslog collector transport security, parsing, buffering, and source identity Existing Elasticsearch Planned migration or reindex process version compatibility, mappings, templates, security, downtime, validation, and rollback

docs.title: Make the onboarding decision
docs.text:
Record:

  1. data owner and classification;
  2. expected events or documents per second and daily volume;
  3. retention and deletion requirements;
  4. approved source and destination network paths;
  5. deployment-derived endpoint and certificate chain;
  6. least-privilege credential owner and rotation interval;
  7. index template, data stream, or integration owner;
  8. failure buffering, retry, and duplicate-handling behavior;
  9. validation queries and dashboards;
  10. support boundary for the source collector or application.

For a complete example, use onboard observability data or onboard search data.

docs.title: Delete the application
docs.text: Deleting the Azure managed application also deletes its managed resource group. Treat deletion as destructive and irreversible unless your recovery plan has been tested.

docs.title: Before deletion
docs.text:
1. Obtain application-owner, data-owner, security, and billing approval.
  2. Stop or redirect ingestion clients.
  3. Export data that must be retained.
  4. Create and verify the required final snapshot.
  5. Confirm where the snapshot is stored and whether deleting the application affects access to it.
  6. Record users, integrations, DNS records, Private Endpoints, certificates, alerts, and dependent applications that must be removed.
  7. Record the managed application resource ID and deletion approval.

docs.title: Delete and monitor
docs.text:
1. In the Azure portal, open the managed application.
  2. Review the resource and managed resource group one final time.
  3. Select the Azure delete action and confirm the exact application.
  4. Monitor the state through Deleting to Deleted.
  5. Do not manually delete individual managed resources to speed up the process.
  6. Escalate if Azure reports deletion failure or managed resources remain after the managed application is gone.

docs.title: Complete decommissioning
docs.text:
• Remove customer-owned Private Endpoints and unused DNS records.
  • Revoke application identities, API keys, and client credentials.
  • Remove monitoring, alerts, allowlists, and integration configuration.
  • Confirm billing and Marketplace subscription state.
  • Retain the approved audit and recovery records without retaining secrets.

Microsoft documents the deletion behavior in Azure Managed Applications overview.

docs.title: Deploy from Azure Marketplace
docs.text: Use the offer and plan approved by procurement and the values completed during planning. The live Marketplace form is authoritative when a field or label differs from this guide.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • completed Azure and Marketplace prerequisites;
  • an approved deployment checklist;
  • permission to create the managed application and required role assignments;
  • the verified offer link or publisher, application, and plan identity.

docs.title: Create the managed application
docs.text:
1. In the Azure portal, open the approved Marketplace offer. Confirm the publisher is iVedha, the product is iVedha Managed Elasticsearch Platform, and the intended plan is selected.
  2. Select Create.
  3. On Basics, select the approved subscription, resource group, region, and application name.
  4. Select the approved workload profile, capacity, topology, and optional machine-learning setting.
  5. Configure the planned public or private connectivity model. Use only network settings supplied or requested by the live form.
  6. Configure the deployment domain and DNS options. Enter only an approved public or private domain and record the DNS owner.
  7. Configure the approved maintenance occurrence, day, start time, time zone, and duration exposed by the plan.
  8. Enter the approved operational or support contacts.
  9. Complete licensing or other plan-specific fields shown by the live form. Do not enter a secret in a free-text, contact, tag, or advanced field.
  10. On Review + create, resolve every validation error and review the configuration, price, terms, permissions, and managed-resource-group settings.
  11. Select Create when the review is correct.

docs.title: Confirm Azure accepted the request
docs.text:
Azure should create a deployment record and managed application resource. Record the application resource ID, region, selected plan and configuration, deployment or correlation ID, and creation time. Do not record secrets.

Warning

Do not edit resources in the managed resource group while provisioning is in progress. Manual changes can be denied, can interrupt reconciliation, and can make the deployment unsupported.

Azure acceptance is not platform readiness. Continue to monitor deployment.

docs.title: Deployment options
docs.text:
The exact labels, allowed values, and ordering depend on the selected offer and plan. The approved live Marketplace form is authoritative. Use this page to understand the decision behind each common option.

Form option What it controls When to choose or enter it Subscription Azure ownership, billing, policy, quota, and tenant boundary Use the subscription approved during planning Resource group Customer-owned location of the managed application resource Use an approved new or existing application resource group Region Azure location for the managed application and supported resources Choose only a region exposed by the approved plan and permitted by policy Application name Customer-visible identity of the managed application Follow the customer's naming standard; do not encode secrets or mutable details Workload profile Search or Observability intent exposed by the plan Choose the profile matching the primary measured workload Capacity Starting ingestion and storage planning range Choose from workload evidence, not from a size label alone Topology Elasticsearch role and data-tier layout Choose the supported availability and tiering model required by the workload Optional ML Additional machine-learning capability when available Enable only with a verified use case, eligible license, and capacity plan Public or private connectivity Customer path to published service endpoints Use the access model approved in the network plan Domain and DNS Public or private service hostname namespace Enter only an approved domain with an assigned DNS and certificate owner Maintenance Controlled maintenance occurrence, day, time, time zone, and duration Use the approved operational window shown by the form Licensing Supported Elastic license selection or material Use only the entitlement and workflow approved for the selected plan Support contacts People who receive deployment or support communication Use monitored business contacts approved for this deployment

Plan-specific identity, tagging, or advanced options can also appear. Use an option only when its purpose, owner, validation, and rollback are documented. Never place a password, private key, access token, connection string, or license secret in a field that is not explicitly designed to protect it.

For the execution sequence, see deploy from Azure Marketplace.

docs.title: Review deployment details
docs.text: Use the managed application's deployment details as the source of truth for resource IDs and endpoint names. Never reconstruct internal resource names from a naming convention.

docs.title: Record the deployment identity
docs.text:
1. In the Azure portal, open Managed applications.
  2. Select the deployed application.
  3. Record the subscription, application resource group, application resource ID, region, and provisioning state.
  4. Open the most recent successful deployment and review Outputs.
  5. Use the managed application view for supported customer-facing properties that are not exposed as ARM outputs.

docs.title: Record connection information
docs.text:
Where present, record:

  • Elasticsearch URL;
  • Kibana URL;
  • Fleet and Logstash URLs if the selected plan exposes them;
  • whether each endpoint is public or private;
  • required service hostnames;
  • the authoritative Private Link Service resource ID;
  • any customer DNS action;
  • certificate or CSR status.

Outputs must not contain secret values. If an output appears to expose a password, token, private key, or connection string, do not copy it into documentation or a ticket. Report it through the approved security process.

docs.title: Verify the outputs
docs.text:
• Hostnames use the approved customer or managed domain.
  • Private endpoints are not expected to work before Private Endpoint, DNS, and TLS configuration is complete.
  • Public endpoints resolve to the expected public path and present a trusted certificate.
  • The recorded Private Link Service resource ID comes directly from deployment details.

Confirm the current application state is ready for customer configuration.

Deployment complete — continue to Next Steps.

docs.title: Monitor deployment
docs.text:
Monitor the Azure deployment and managed application until all platform readiness gates complete. ARM success is not the same as platform readiness.

Azure resource success is one gate in the managed-platform lifecycle, not the final readiness signal.

docs.title: Follow the readiness gates
docs.text: Gate Evidence Continue when 1. Marketplace accepted Azure create request and deployment record Azure accepted the requested deployment 2. ARM deployment succeeded Application resource-group deployment operations All required ARM operations report Succeeded 3. Managed application reconciliation Health and Sync Status in the customer view The managed application reports the desired state 4. Elasticsearch and Kibana ready Customer-visible platform health Both services report ready 5. Endpoints published Deployment outputs or customer-facing properties Authoritative URLs, domains, and required identifiers are present 6. Customer post-deployment work Next Steps verification Network, DNS, TLS, and authentication checks succeed

docs.title: Open the managed application
docs.text:
1. In the Azure portal, search for Managed applications.
  2. Select the application and confirm its name, subscription, resource group, region, and provisioning state.
  3. Open the application resource group and review Deployments. If an operation is active, wait rather than starting a duplicate.
  4. Under Resources, open My Deployment when available.
  5. Review Profile, Capacity, Topology, Location, Health, Sync Status, and More Info. Do not infer readiness from one column.
  6. Record the first time the platform reaches the endpoint-publication gate.

docs.title: Use only supported actions
docs.text: Managed actions can include certificate management, DNS guidance, support, and controlled deployment configuration. Use an action only when it appears in the deployed application. Do not modify managed infrastructure to reproduce an absent action.

docs.title: Respond to a stopped or failed deployment
docs.text:
Wait while progress is changing. Follow deployment troubleshooting when Azure reports Failed, progress stops with no active operation, endpoints never appear, or services remain unavailable after reconciliation.

When endpoints are published, continue to review deployment details.

docs.title: Contact support
docs.text:
Use Request Support in the deployed managed application or the contact shown in its approved Marketplace listing. A source-code portal URL or internal channel is not an approved customer support route unless it appears there.

Keep one support record from initial impact through customer-validated closure.

docs.title: Submit through the managed application
docs.text:
1. Open the managed application Overview.
  2. Select Request Support.
  3. Enter Your Email Address.
  4. Enter a concise Request Subject.
  5. In Request Description, state the impact, start time, affected users or services, exact symptom, and troubleshooting already completed.
  6. Review the form for credentials, personal data, and customer content.
  7. Submit the request and retain the resulting reference.

docs.title: Classify the impact
docs.text:
Use the severity term defined in the approved Marketplace support agreement. If the agreement uses P1–P4, classify impact consistently:

Severity Customer impact example P1 critical Production service unavailable, widespread data ingestion stopped, or active security impact with no workaround P2 high Major production function degraded or a material group blocked with no acceptable workaround P3 medium Limited degradation, non-critical function affected, or an acceptable workaround exists P4 low Information request, documentation question, or planned change guidance

This table helps describe impact; it does not create a response-time commitment. Support hours, initial-response targets, escalation intervals, and service exclusions come from the approved offer or service agreement.

docs.title: Include
docs.text:
• managed application resource ID;
  • subscription and application resource group names when approved for sharing;
  • deployment region and plan;
  • problem start time and time zone;
  • exact user-visible symptom;
  • affected endpoint or operation without credentials;
  • whether one or all users and networks are affected;
  • last known successful time;
  • Azure deployment or correlation ID;
  • redacted error code and message;
  • diagnostic steps already completed;
  • business impact and required response time.

Use this subject pattern:

[P1-P4] <application name> - <region> - <short symptom>

Use this description structure:

Impact:
Started:
Last known good:
Affected users, sources, or endpoints:
Observed error:
Expected result:
Recent approved change:
Checks completed:
Correlation or deployment ID:
Safe attachment list:
Contact and time zone:

docs.title: Do not include
docs.text:
• passwords, one-time passwords, API keys, tokens, cookies, or headers;
  • private keys or complete certificate bundles;
  • unredacted ARM parameters or environment dumps;
  • customer documents, indexed records, or personal information;
  • credential-bearing Git remotes or internal automation endpoints.

If the issue is an Azure purchasing, subscription, policy, or platform-service problem rather than application behavior, use the Azure support path approved by your organization.

docs.title: Escalation and communications
docs.text:
• Use the ticket reference for updates; do not split one incident across unapproved channels.
  • State immediately when impact or scope increases.
  • Ask for an escalation through the support route when the response target in the approved agreement is missed.
  • Record maintenance, workaround, recovery, and closure decisions.
  • For a suspected credential or data exposure, use the approved security incident route rather than attaching sensitive evidence to a normal ticket.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Application resource group Customer-controlled resource group containing the managed application   resource. Azure Managed Application Azure resource that packages a supported application and its managed   infrastructure. Elasticsearch Distributed search and analytics engine that indexes and queries data. Kibana Elastic user interface for exploring, visualizing, and administering data and   supported cluster features. Managed resource group Resource group containing application infrastructure governed by the managed   application definition. Private Endpoint Customer-owned network interface that gives a service a private IP in a VNet. Private Link Service Service-side Azure resource to which an approved Private Endpoint connects. Private DNS DNS namespace visible to approved private networks that maps service   hostnames to private endpoint addresses. Snapshot Elasticsearch backup stored in an off-cluster snapshot repository. Subject alternative name Certificate field listing the hostnames for which the certificate is valid. TLS Protocol that encrypts a connection and verifies service identity through a   certificate and trust chain.

docs.title: Monitor health and capacity
docs.text:
Monitor both customer workloads and managed-service readiness. A green Azure resource state does not prove that ingestion, search, or every Elasticsearch index is healthy.

A monitoring agent in the managed resource group forwards operational platform telemetry to the iVedha monitoring cluster. iVedha uses this telemetry to monitor supported platform health. Customers remain responsible for verifying workload outcomes, data quality, ingestion completeness, dashboards, and application-level service objectives.

docs.title: Review cluster health
docs.text:
With an appropriately privileged user:

curl --fail-with-body --user "<user>" \
  "https://<elasticsearch-hostname>/_cluster/health?pretty"

Review:

  • cluster status and unassigned shards;
  • node availability;
  • disk use and growth;
  • indexing rejection or latency;
  • search latency and errors;
  • shard count and size;
  • snapshot failures;
  • Kibana and client availability.

docs.title: Respond to disk pressure
docs.text:
Elasticsearch uses disk watermarks to protect nodes. At the flood-stage watermark it can block writes to affected indices. Do not permanently raise watermarks to hide insufficient capacity.

  1. Confirm which nodes and indices are affected.
  2. Stop avoidable ingestion bursts.
  3. Delete data only under an approved retention decision.
  4. Request a supported capacity or topology change when growth is durable.
  5. Confirm that write blocks clear and ingestion recovers.

See Elastic watermark errors for current product behavior.

docs.title: Request a capacity change
docs.text: Provide current capacity, observed growth, retention, peak ingestion, query load, shard metrics, business deadline, and the requested outcome. Do not ask for a size label without supporting workload evidence.

docs.title: Manage the Elastic license
docs.text: Elastic features depend on the active license and deployment configuration. The source package supports Basic, trial, and supplied commercial-license paths, but the options available to you depend on the approved offer and plan.

docs.title: Check license status
docs.text:
Use an authorized account:

curl --fail-with-body --user "<user>" \
  "https://<elasticsearch-hostname>/_license"

Record the license type, status, and expiration when present. Do not copy a license file or credential into a ticket.

docs.title: Change license configuration
docs.text:
1. Confirm the commercial entitlement and the features that require it.
  2. Confirm that the managed application exposes a license action.
  3. Store the supplied license material only through that protected action.
  4. Submit the change and wait for it to complete.
  5. Recheck the Elasticsearch license API.
  6. Test one required licensed feature with a least-privilege account.

Do not install an undocumented command-line tool, place license material in source control, or infer a license from the Marketplace plan name.

If the action is unavailable or the license is rejected, preserve the API status and error text after removing sensitive values, then get support.

docs.title: Lifecycle states
docs.text:
State Customer meaning Terminal? Accepted Azure accepted the requested lifecycle action No Succeeded Azure completed the reported resource action Not necessarily service-ready Failed The current create or delete episode failed Yes for that episode Deleting Deprovisioning is active No Deleted The managed application is absent Yes

The managed service can continue readiness checks after ARM reports Succeeded. Treat the application as ready only when authoritative endpoints, health, access, and the documented readiness result are available.

Repeated or delayed events are an implementation concern, not a reason for a customer to create duplicate applications or edit managed resources.

See follow deployment status for the customer procedure.

docs.title: Manage maintenance
docs.text: The deployment can record a maintenance schedule for coordinated platform changes. Use the managed application action only when it is available for the deployed plan.

docs.title: Prepare for maintenance
docs.text:
1. Confirm the occurrence, weekday, start time, time zone, and duration shown by the deployment.
  2. Identify affected users, ingestion pipelines, and client retry behavior.
  3. Review service health and active incidents.
  4. Verify a recent usable snapshot when the change can affect data.
  5. Communicate the expected impact through approved channels.

docs.title: Update the schedule
docs.text:
1. Open the managed application in the Azure portal.
  2. Open the supported maintenance configuration action.
  3. Enter the approved schedule and time zone.
  4. Review the value carefully; do not infer local time from UTC.
  5. Submit the change and record its operation or change identifier.
  6. Wait for the action to complete before submitting another schedule change.

docs.title: Validate afterward
docs.text:
• Elasticsearch cluster health is acceptable.
  • Kibana loads and users can authenticate.
  • Ingestion and searches have recovered.
  • No unexpected certificate, DNS, or license warning is present.
  • The managed application shows the intended schedule.

If the maintenance action is missing, the schedule does not update, or service health degrades, collect safe evidence and get support.

docs.title: Azure and Marketplace prerequisites
docs.text: Complete these checks with your Azure billing, subscription, identity, and network administrators before opening the deployment form.

docs.title: Marketplace and billing
docs.text:
1. Confirm that Microsoft Marketplace purchases are enabled for the billing account and subscription.
  2. Confirm that the deploying user may purchase or accept the approved offer.
  3. If your organization uses Private Marketplace, confirm that the offer and plan are allowed.
  4. Use the offer link or offer identity approved by your procurement team. Do not choose a similarly named listing.

Microsoft documents the current purchasing controls in Enable Marketplace purchases.

docs.title: Permissions and ownership
docs.text:
The deploying identity needs permission to create a managed application and its application resource group. The deployment can also require permission to create role assignments for managed identities. Private Endpoint and DNS work can belong to separate resource groups and owners.

Do not assume that an Azure Contributor role can create every required role assignment. Ask an Azure administrator to validate the deployment against your tenant's RBAC and policy design.

docs.title: Subscription readiness
docs.text:
Confirm:

  • the target subscription and Microsoft Entra tenant;
  • the approved Azure region;
  • sufficient compute, storage, networking, and public IP quota for the chosen deployment;
  • required Azure resource providers are registered;
  • Azure Policy permits the resource types and selected region;
  • naming and tagging requirements;
  • a resource group for the managed application;
  • customer contacts who can receive deployment and support communication.

docs.title: Confirm readiness
docs.text:
Confirm that the approved plan is supported in the selected region and that the responsible teams own every required subscription-, network-, DNS-, and identity-scoped action. The live Marketplace offer and Azure subscription are authoritative for current plan and region availability.

Choose the access model in plan connectivity, then record the approved values in the planning overview.

docs.title: Plan connectivity
docs.text:
Choose one access model before deployment. This page covers the decision and required owners; configuration steps begin in Next Steps.

Public access uses an internet-reachable endpoint. Private access requires a customer network route, private DNS, a Private Endpoint, and the deployment's Private Link path.

docs.title: Choose the access model
docs.text:
Decision Public access Private access Endpoint Internet-reachable service endpoint Private Endpoint in a customer subnet Client path Approved internet or proxy path VNet, peering, VPN, or ExpressRoute route to the endpoint DNS Authoritative public records Private zone plus VNet links or hybrid forwarding TLS Certificate valid for every public service hostname Customer certificate or CA workflow when required for the private domain Restrictions Deployment-supported source, proxy, or firewall controls Customer routing, network security, and endpoint approval controls Best fit Security policy permits public reachability Clients must remain on approved private networks

Authentication and authorization are required in both models. Do not choose public access merely to avoid private DNS or route planning.

docs.title: Plan public access
docs.text:
Confirm that:

  • internet-reachable endpoints are approved;
  • the public DNS zone and record owner are known;
  • the certificate owner can issue or approve certificates for every hostname;
  • approved source restrictions, proxy controls, and firewall rules are documented;
  • users and clients will authenticate with named, least-privilege identities.

docs.title: Plan private access
docs.text:
Confirm that:

  • the customer VNet and Private Endpoint subnet have non-overlapping, available address space;
  • every client network has an approved route to that subnet;
  • the Private Endpoint and connection-approval owners are known;
  • Azure-native and hybrid DNS clients have a supported resolution path;
  • the private DNS zone and certificate-authority owners are known;
  • the certificate workflow can cover every deployment-provided hostname.

Do not reconstruct a Private Link Service resource ID or internal resource name. Obtain the authoritative identifier from deployment details after the platform is ready.

docs.title: Keep the access layers separate
docs.text:
1. Private Endpoint and routing provide the private network path.
  2. DNS maps a service hostname to the intended endpoint.
  3. TLS verifies hostname identity and certificate trust.
  4. Authentication verifies the user or client.

An IP address is not a substitute for the service hostname because TLS validates the hostname. Record the selected model and each owner in the planning overview.

docs.title: Next steps overview
docs.text: Start these tasks only after the managed application is ready and its authoritative endpoints and identifiers are published. Complete the path that matches the access model recorded in deployment details.

docs.title: Public deployment
docs.text:
1. Reset the administrator password.
  2. Configure and verify public network access.
  3. Create the deployment-provided public DNS records when a custom domain is used.
  4. Configure the required TLS certificate when the managed application exposes a customer-certificate action.
  5. Verify Elasticsearch and Kibana access.

docs.title: Private deployment
docs.text:
1. Reset the administrator password.
  2. Create a Private Endpoint.
  3. Verify the route from every approved client network to the endpoint.
  4. Configure private DNS.
  5. Configure the required TLS certificate.
  6. Verify Elasticsearch and Kibana access.

Do not bypass DNS or TLS with an IP address, a hosts-file entry, or disabled certificate verification. When the verification page succeeds, the platform is ready for least-privilege access and production data onboarding.

docs.title: Onboard observability data
docs.text:
Use an OpenTelemetry Collector in gateway mode so applications send to a customer-operated collector that can batch, retry, and control egress. This procedure applies only when the deployment's Elasticsearch version supports the OTLP/HTTP endpoint.

Applications send telemetry to a customer-operated Collector. The Collector uses the deployment-provided HTTPS endpoint; telemetry remains in the customer's Azure-hosted managed platform.

docs.title: Choose the supported intake path
docs.text:
Do not treat all Elastic OpenTelemetry endpoints as interchangeable:

Path When to use it Direct Elasticsearch OTLP/HTTP Use this tutorial only after confirming the deployed Elasticsearch version exposes /_otlp/v1/logs, /_otlp/v1/metrics, and /_otlp/v1/traces Customer-operated Collector Recommended gateway for batching, retry, egress control, and limiting application connection churn APM Server OTLP intake Use only when the deployment explicitly exposes and supports an APM Server endpoint; its protocol and paths differ Elastic Agent and Fleet Use when Fleet and the required integration are exposed and compatible with the deployed Elastic version

The direct Elasticsearch endpoint accepts OTLP/HTTP with protobuf encoding. It does not accept OTLP/gRPC. Do not send OTLP to Kibana, omit the /_otlp base path, or guess that a Cloud-hosted or APM endpoint exists.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Confirm:

  • the deployment-derived Elasticsearch URL;
  • OTLP/HTTP support for the deployed version;
  • TCP 443, DNS, and TLS trust from the collector;
  • an administrator who can create a scoped API key;
  • a non-production source for the first validation;
  • ownership for collector availability, buffering, and upgrades.

docs.title: Create a least-privilege API key
docs.text:
Set the endpoint without credentials:

export ELASTICSEARCH_URL="https://<deployment-elasticsearch-hostname>"

Using an approved administrator credential, create an expiring onboarding key:

curl --fail-with-body --user "<api-key-administrator>" \
  --request POST "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/_security/api_key" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "name": "otel-gateway",
    "expiration": "30d",
    "role_descriptors": {
      "otel_writer": {
        "indices": [
          {
            "names": ["logs-*", "metrics-*", "traces-*"],
            "privileges": ["auto_configure", "create_doc"]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  }'

Enter the administrator password through the client prompt. Store the returned encoded API key in the approved secret store; do not place it in a file, screenshot, shell history, or ticket.

docs.title: Configure the Collector
docs.text:
Use environment substitution for the endpoint and secret:

receivers:
  otlp:
    protocols:
      http:

processors:
  batch: {}
  memory_limiter:
    check_interval: 1s
    limit_mib: 512

exporters:
  otlphttp/elastic:
    endpoint: ${env:ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/_otlp
    headers:
      Authorization: "ApiKey ${env:ELASTIC_API_KEY}"

service:
  pipelines:
    logs:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/elastic]
    metrics:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/elastic]
    traces:
      receivers: [otlp]
      processors: [memory_limiter, batch]
      exporters: [otlphttp/elastic]

Pin a Collector version supported by your organization. Add persistent buffering, high availability, resource limits, and telemetry for the Collector before production use.

The exporter appends /v1/logs, /v1/metrics, or /v1/traces to the /_otlp base path. Follow the Elastic Elasticsearch OTLP/HTTP endpoint guidance for the deployed version rather than copying configuration for Elastic Cloud Managed OTLP or APM Server.

docs.title: Verify and hand over
docs.text:
1. Send one synthetic log, metric, and trace from a test source.
  2. Confirm the Collector reports successful export without retry or TLS errors.
  3. In Kibana, confirm logs-*, metrics-*, and traces-* data streams appear only for the signals sent.
  4. Verify timestamps, service identity, environment, and sensitive-field handling.
  5. Test Collector restart and destination unavailability behavior.
  6. Record the API-key owner and rotation date.

Revoke the test key if the onboarding is abandoned. For endpoint or TLS failures, follow connectivity troubleshooting.

docs.title: Onboard search data
docs.text: This tutorial creates a synthetic docs-search-default data stream. Use a separate naming, mapping, lifecycle, and relevance design for production data.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • the deployment-derived Elasticsearch URL;
  • working DNS and TLS;
  • an administrator with permission to create index templates and API keys;
  • approval to create and delete tutorial resources.

Set the endpoint without embedding credentials:

export ELASTICSEARCH_URL="https://<deployment-elasticsearch-hostname>"

docs.title: Create the data-stream template
docs.text:
curl --fail-with-body --user "<search-administrator>" \
  --request PUT "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/_index_template/docs-search-template" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "index_patterns": ["docs-search-*"],
    "data_stream": {},
    "template": {
      "mappings": {
        "properties": {
          "@timestamp": {"type": "date"},
          "title": {"type": "text"},
          "body": {"type": "text"},
          "source_id": {"type": "keyword"}
        }
      }
    }
  }'

Confirm the response contains "acknowledged":true.

docs.title: Create the writer API key
docs.text:
curl --fail-with-body --user "<api-key-administrator>" \
  --request POST "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/_security/api_key" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "name": "docs-search-writer",
    "expiration": "7d",
    "role_descriptors": {
      "docs_search_writer": {
        "indices": [
          {
            "names": ["docs-search-*"],
            "privileges": ["auto_configure", "create_doc"]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  }'

Confirm that the response contains an API-key ID and encoded key. Store both in the approved secret store.

docs.title: Create the validation API key
docs.text:
Use a separate read-only identity for the tutorial search:

curl --fail-with-body --user "<api-key-administrator>" \
  --request POST "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/_security/api_key" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "name": "docs-search-validator",
    "expiration": "7d",
    "role_descriptors": {
      "docs_search_validator": {
        "indices": [
          {
            "names": ["docs-search-*"],
            "privileges": ["read"]
          }
        ]
      }
    }
  }'

Store the validation key and its ID separately from the writer key. A production ingestion identity normally does not need read.

docs.title: Load the keys without echoing them
docs.text:
Retrieve the encoded values from the approved secret store and enter them at the prompts:

IFS= read -rsp "Writer API key: " ELASTIC_WRITE_API_KEY
printf "\n"
IFS= read -rsp "Validation API key: " ELASTIC_READ_API_KEY
printf "\n"

The secret input is not echoed and is not part of the command stored in Bash history. Do not export either variable, save it in a shell profile, or enter the value directly on a command line.

docs.title: Index and search a document
docs.text:
curl --fail-with-body \
  --request POST \
  "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/docs-search-default/_doc?op_type=create&refresh=wait_for" \
  --header "Authorization: ApiKey ${ELASTIC_WRITE_API_KEY}" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "@timestamp": "2026-07-29T00:00:00Z",
    "title": "Synthetic onboarding document",
    "body": "This document validates the managed search ingestion path.",
    "source_id": "docs-tutorial-001"
  }'

Confirm the response reports "result":"created", then search:

curl --fail-with-body \
  "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/docs-search-default/_search?q=source_id:docs-tutorial-001" \
  --header "Authorization: ApiKey ${ELASTIC_READ_API_KEY}"

The response must contain exactly the synthetic document. Remove the keys from the current shell immediately after validation:

unset ELASTIC_WRITE_API_KEY ELASTIC_READ_API_KEY

docs.title: Clean up
docs.text:
Delete the tutorial data stream and template with an approved administrator, then invalidate the API key:

curl --fail-with-body --user "<search-administrator>" \
  --request DELETE "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/_data_stream/docs-search-default"

curl --fail-with-body --user "<search-administrator>" \
  --request DELETE "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/_index_template/docs-search-template"

Use both API-key IDs returned at creation time with the invalidate API. Do not reuse either tutorial key for production.

docs.title: Operations overview
docs.text: Use the managed application view, Elasticsearch and Kibana product interfaces, and approved support actions. Do not modify the managed infrastructure directly.

docs.title: Daily
docs.text:
• Check service availability and important ingestion failures.
  • Review cluster health and capacity alerts.
  • Investigate authentication or certificate warnings.

docs.title: Weekly
docs.text:
• Review data growth, shard health, query performance, and failed jobs.
  • Confirm that snapshot operations are succeeding where configured.
  • Review open deployment or support actions.

docs.title: Before a planned change
docs.text:
• Confirm ownership, scope, risk, validation, rollback, and maintenance timing.
  • Take or verify a usable snapshot when the change can affect data.
  • Test access with a non-administrator account after the change.

docs.title: Supported tasks
docs.text:
• Manage users and roles
  • Configure single sign-on
  • Choose a data onboarding path
  • Search and visualize data
  • Monitor health and capacity
  • Manage maintenance
  • Manage the Elastic license
  • Back up and restore
  • Prepare for upgrades
  • Renew TLS certificates
  • Delete the application

Record customer-visible changes and their validation results. Never place passwords, access tokens, private keys, or unredacted diagnostics in the change record.

docs.title: Platform components
docs.text:
The platform release deploys twelve component applications. This page provides one customer-facing description and one stable documentation anchor for each application.

The application identifiers are implementation identifiers, not Azure resource names. Do not use them to reconstruct resource IDs, hostnames, credentials, or other deployment-specific values. Obtain those values from deployment outputs.

docs.title: One-to-one component map
docs.text:
Argo CD application Customer-facing purpose Availability computed-values Produces the approved configuration values consumed by the other component applications Every deployment deployment-postrequisites Completes release-defined configuration and readiness work after the main services are deployed Every deployment deployment-prerequisites Establishes release-defined dependencies and readiness gates required before the main services deploy Every deployment elastic-connectors Supplies supported Elastic connector services for approved external content or service integrations Plan, version, license, and configuration dependent elasticsearch Stores, indexes, searches, and analyzes customer data Every deployment fleet-server Coordinates enrolled Elastic Agents through Fleet Plan and configuration dependent infrastructure Supplies the shared Azure runtime, storage, identity, and networking foundation Every deployment ingress Presents approved HTTPS endpoints for enabled platform services Every deployment kibana Provides the browser interface for search, dashboards, administration, and enabled Elastic solutions Every deployment logstash Receives and processes events through configured input, filter, and output pipelines Plan and configuration dependent elastic-agent Runs the platform-managed Elastic Agent workload and its approved policy Release and configuration dependent secrets Supplies protected secret and certificate material required by platform services Every deployment

A component listed as plan-dependent is not available merely because its Argo CD application exists in platform source. Confirm the deployed plan, version, license, status, and published endpoint before using it.

docs.title: Computed values
docs.text:
Argo CD application: computed-values

Computed values derives the shared, release-approved configuration consumed by other component applications. Its customer-facing result is consistent configuration across the deployment, including values later exposed through supported status and output views.

Customers do not edit generated values or use this application as a source for resource names. Change deployment configuration only through a documented managed-application action.

Path and anchor: /elastic/latest/elastic-stack-deployment/platform-components/#component-computed-values

docs.title: Deployment postrequisites
docs.text:
Argo CD application: deployment-postrequisites

Deployment postrequisites performs the release-defined configuration and readiness work that can run only after the main platform services are present. The exact tasks are version-specific; the customer-facing outcome is a platform that can advance from infrastructure deployment toward service readiness.

Customers should follow the managed application's readiness state rather than attempting to run or modify individual post-deployment tasks.

Path and anchor: /elastic/latest/elastic-stack-deployment/platform-components/#component-deployment-postrequisites

docs.title: Deployment prerequisites
docs.text:
Argo CD application: deployment-prerequisites

Deployment prerequisites establishes the release-defined dependencies and readiness gates required before Elasticsearch and the other main services can be configured. The customer-facing outcome is early validation of the foundation required by the selected plan.

When this component does not become ready, review the managed application's status and deployment evidence. Do not bypass the gate by changing managed resources directly.

Path and anchor: /elastic/latest/elastic-stack-deployment/platform-components/#component-deployment-prerequisites

docs.title: Elastic connectors
docs.text:
Argo CD application: elastic-connectors

Elastic connectors supplies the connector service used by supported Elastic workflows that synchronize content or interact with approved external systems. A deployed connector service does not automatically configure a data source, credential, synchronization job, or external model provider.

Before use, verify the selected connector, Elastic version and license, outbound connectivity, credential owner, source permissions, and data classification. Elastic documents connector behavior in the Elasticsearch connectors reference.

Path and anchor: /elastic/latest/elastic-stack-deployment/platform-components/#component-elastic-connectors

docs.title: Elasticsearch
docs.text:
Argo CD application: elasticsearch

Elasticsearch is the platform's distributed search and analytics engine, scalable data store, and vector database. It stores customer indices and data streams and provides APIs for indexing, search, aggregations, ingest pipelines, security, and supported lifecycle operations.

Customers own mappings, templates, data streams, retention, API access, query behavior, and data governance. Use the deployment-provided Elasticsearch hostname rather than an internal Kubernetes or Azure address. See the official Elasticsearch reference.

Path and anchor: /elastic/latest/elastic-stack-deployment/platform-components/#component-elasticsearch

docs.title: Fleet Server
docs.text:
Argo CD application: fleet-server

Fleet Server is the control-plane service through which enrolled Elastic Agents receive policies and report status to Fleet. Collected events are stored in Elasticsearch, not in Fleet Server.

Use this component only when deployment outputs expose an approved Fleet endpoint. Customers remain responsible for their agent installations, source permissions, certificate trust, policy approval, and compatible versions. See Fleet and Elastic Agent.

Path and anchor: /elastic/latest/elastic-stack-deployment/platform-components/#component-fleet-server

docs.title: Infrastructure
docs.text:
Argo CD application: infrastructure

Infrastructure supplies the shared Azure foundation consumed by the platform services. Depending on the approved release, that foundation can include the managed runtime, storage, identities, and networking resources represented in the managed resource group.

The exact resource inventory is release-specific. Customers own the Azure subscription, policy, quota, approved connectivity, and Azure charges, but must not modify individual managed resources unless a documented action explicitly permits it.

Path and anchor: /elastic/latest/elastic-stack-deployment/platform-components/#component-infrastructure

docs.title: Ingress
docs.text:
Argo CD application: ingress

Ingress presents the approved HTTPS routes for enabled services such as Elasticsearch, Kibana, Fleet Server, or Logstash. It connects the platform's internal service routing to the public or private access model selected for the deployment.

Customers configure the required network path, DNS, TLS trust, and client access. The deployment-provided service hostname remains authoritative; do not connect clients to an internal load balancer, pod, or Kubernetes service name.

Path and anchor: /elastic/latest/elastic-stack-deployment/platform-components/#component-ingress

docs.title: Kibana
docs.text:
Argo CD application: kibana

Kibana is the browser interface for exploring data, creating dashboards and visualizations, administering supported Elasticsearch features, managing access, and using enabled Elastic solutions.

Kibana reads from and administers Elasticsearch; it is not a separate copy of the customer's indexed data. Customers use the deployment-provided Kibana hostname and receive only the privileges assigned to their identity.

Path and anchor: /elastic/latest/elastic-stack-deployment/platform-components/#component-kibana

docs.title: Logstash
docs.text:
Argo CD application: logstash

Logstash receives, transforms, enriches, buffers, and routes events through configured input, filter, and output pipeline stages. It is useful when an ingestion flow needs processing beyond a direct Elasticsearch API or an approved agent integration.

Use the managed Logstash service only when the selected plan publishes a supported endpoint and pipeline workflow. Customers own source behavior, pipeline requirements, parsing validation, credential rotation, and failure handling. See how Logstash works.

Path and anchor: /elastic/latest/elastic-stack-deployment/platform-components/#component-logstash

docs.title: Elastic Agent
docs.text:
Argo CD application: elastic-agent

This application deploys the platform-managed Elastic Agent workload and its approved policy. Its purpose and enabled integrations depend on the platform release and configuration.

This component is distinct from Elastic Agents that customers install on their own hosts or Kubernetes clusters. Customers operate those external agents and must verify Fleet enrollment, endpoint reachability, version compatibility, resource use, and source permissions.

Path and anchor: /elastic/latest/elastic-stack-deployment/platform-components/#component-elastic-agent

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
Argo CD application: secrets

Secrets supplies the protected secret, key, and certificate material required by platform services and supported TLS or integration workflows. Secret values must not appear in deployment outputs, documentation, source control, or support evidence.

Customers use only documented certificate, identity, or credential actions. Do not read, replace, or copy secret material directly from managed resources.

Path and anchor: /elastic/latest/elastic-stack-deployment/platform-components/#component-secrets

docs.title: Verify a component
docs.text:
For any component:

  1. Confirm that the component is included in the approved Marketplace plan.
  2. Check the managed application's platform version and readiness state.
  3. Use deployment outputs to find customer-facing endpoints or required actions.
  4. Confirm the Elastic version, license, and compatibility where applicable.
  5. Record the customer and iVedha ownership boundary.
  6. Treat the component as unavailable until all required evidence is present.

For placement and data flow, see the architecture and deployment model. For customer and operator responsibilities, see shared responsibility.

docs.title: Planning overview
docs.text: Complete the deployment decisions before opening Azure Marketplace. Use values approved by the teams that own the Azure subscription, workload, network, identity, and operations; do not copy values from another environment.

docs.title: Make the deployment decisions
docs.text:
Decision Example considerations Record Azure subscription Microsoft Entra tenant, subscription, Azure region, policy, quota, and billing owner Approved tenant, subscription, and region Capacity Small, Medium, or Large choice exposed by the approved plan Expected daily ingestion, searchable data, retention, and query demand Topology Supported all-in-one or role-separated topology Availability, data-tiering, and scale requirements Connectivity Public or private access Client locations, exposure policy, routing, and firewall ownership DNS Public or private zone ownership Authoritative zone, record owner, and hybrid forwarding when required TLS Public CA or customer CA Required hostnames, certificate workflow, trust, and renewal owner Maintenance Window and time zone Approved occurrence, day, start time, time zone, and duration Support Operational contacts Service owner, technical contact, security contact, and escalation route

Use Azure and Marketplace prerequisites to validate subscription readiness. Use choose capacity and topology and plan connectivity for the two design decisions that need workload and network evidence.

docs.title: Record workload and ownership inputs
docs.text:
Before selecting a capacity profile, record:

  • primary use case: search, observability, analytics, or mixed;
  • expected daily ingestion and searchable data volume;
  • retention and recovery objectives;
  • expected concurrent users, query pattern, and latency objective;
  • data, identity, certificate, snapshot, and decommissioning owners.

docs.title: Confirm readiness
docs.text:
Proceed to Marketplace only when each decision has an approved value and owner. Use the deployment checklist for the final review.

If a deployment-specific value is unknown, resolve it with the owning customer team or iVedha support. Do not invent resource IDs, DNS targets, hostnames, capacity guarantees, or internal resource names.

docs.title: Create a Private Endpoint
docs.text: A Private Endpoint places a network interface with a private IP in a customer subnet and connects it to the deployment's Private Link Service.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • the authoritative Private Link Service resource ID from deployment outputs;
  • permission to create a Private Endpoint in the selected resource group and subnet;
  • an approved VNet and subnet with available address space;
  • a route from the intended client networks.

Warning

Never reconstruct the Private Link Service resource ID from a resource-name pattern. Internal Azure names can change. Use the value from deployment details or obtain it from iVedha support.

docs.title: Create the endpoint
docs.text:
1. In the Azure portal, search for Private endpoints.
  2. Select Create.
  3. On Basics, choose the subscription and resource group that will own the endpoint. Enter an approved name and region.
  4. On Resource, choose the option to connect by resource ID or alias.
  5. Paste the complete Private Link Service resource ID from deployment details.
  6. On Virtual Network, select the approved VNet and subnet.
  7. Configure application security groups or tags only when required by your organization.
  8. Review the settings and select Create.

docs.title: Confirm connection approval
docs.text:
1. Open the created Private Endpoint.
  2. Check Connection status.
  3. If it is Pending, ask the owner shown in deployment details or iVedha support to review the request. Same-subscription requests are not guaranteed to be automatically approved.
  4. Continue only when the status is Approved.

Record the endpoint resource ID, network interface, private IP, subnet, and approval time. Do not publish these deployment-specific values.

The endpoint does not configure application DNS or TLS. Continue with configure private DNS.

docs.title: Configure private DNS
docs.text: Private DNS maps each service hostname to the Private Endpoint's private IP. Use the exact hostnames and private domain from deployment details.

docs.title: Gather authoritative values
docs.text:
Record:

  • Elasticsearch, Kibana, and any other private service hostnames;
  • the Private Endpoint private IP;
  • the VNet from which clients query DNS;
  • the authoritative private DNS zone or corporate DNS owner.

Do not assume a privatelink.* zone name. This application can use a deployment-specific private domain.

docs.title: Azure-native DNS
docs.text:
1. Create or select the Azure Private DNS zone that is authoritative for the deployment's private domain.
  2. Link the zone to every VNet whose clients must resolve the names.
  3. For each hostname supplied by the deployment, create the required record pointing to the Private Endpoint IP. Derive the record label from the authoritative hostname, not from an internal resource name.
  4. Disable VM autoregistration unless the zone has a separate documented need for it.

  5. Query each hostname from a client in a linked VNet:

    nslookup <service-hostname>

  6. Confirm the response is the Private Endpoint's private IP.

docs.title: Hybrid DNS
docs.text:
For on-premises or custom-DNS clients:

  1. Keep the Azure Private DNS zone linked to the endpoint VNet.
  2. Configure a supported Azure DNS forwarding path, such as Azure DNS Private Resolver, from the corporate DNS service.
  3. Add a conditional forwarder for the deployment's private domain.
  4. Test from both an Azure client and an on-premises client.

Do not forward on-premises queries directly to Azure's platform virtual IP. Use a supported resolver reachable from the client network.

docs.title: Validate the result
docs.text:
DNS is complete when every documented service hostname resolves to the private IP from every approved client network. If it returns NXDOMAIN, a public IP, or an old private IP, follow connectivity troubleshooting.

Next, configure private TLS.

docs.title: Configure TLS certificates
docs.text:
Use this workflow when the managed application exposes a certificate action for the selected public or private domain. The supported workflow retains the private key in the managed platform and gives the customer a certificate signing request (CSR) to approve and sign.

The private key remains in the managed platform. Exchange only the CSR and signed public certificate chain.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • working network access and DNS for the selected access model;
  • every exact service hostname from deployment details;
  • access to the certificate action exposed by the managed application;
  • an approved public or private certificate authority trusted by every client;
  • the certificate formats accepted by the live upload action.

The certificate must include every required Elasticsearch, Kibana, and other published service hostname as a subject alternative name (SAN). A wildcard is acceptable only when both the customer certificate policy and upload action support it.

docs.title: Issue and upload the certificate
docs.text:
1. In the managed application, open Certificate Management or the equivalent certificate action exposed by the deployed version.
  2. Select the public or private scope that matches the deployment endpoint.
  3. Download the generated CSR.
  4. Inspect the CSR and confirm that its SANs cover every hostname supplied in deployment details.
  5. Submit the CSR to the approved certificate authority.
  6. Obtain the issued leaf certificate and required intermediate certificates in the encoding and chain order required by the upload action.
  7. Upload the public certificate chain through the same managed action.
  8. Wait for the action and platform synchronization to complete.

Do not upload, export, or send a private key. The managed platform retains the key used to create the CSR and checks that the returned certificate matches it.

docs.title: Validate the certificate
docs.text:
Repeat this check for every service hostname:

SERVICE_HOSTNAME="<deployment-service-hostname>"

openssl s_client \
  -connect "${SERVICE_HOSTNAME}:443" \
  -servername "${SERVICE_HOSTNAME}" \
  -verify_return_error </dev/null

Confirm that:

  • the command ends with Verify return code: 0 (ok);
  • the certificate is within its validity period;
  • the service hostname is present in the SAN extension;
  • the chain ends at a CA trusted by the client.

Do not disable certificate verification. A name-resolution error belongs to DNS; a timeout or refusal belongs to the network path; an issuer or hostname error belongs to certificate issuance, upload, or trust.

Continue with verify access.

docs.title: Choose capacity and topology
docs.text:
The Marketplace form can expose workload, capacity, topology, and optional feature choices. The available combinations depend on the approved offer and plan.

The current Marketplace source defines the following planning choices. Confirm that the same labels and descriptions appear in the approved live offer before using them.

docs.title: Workload profiles
docs.text: Profile Marketplace intent Planning evidence to collect Observability Logs, metrics, and traces Daily ingest, event size, retention, query patterns, dashboards, and concurrent users Search Full-text, vector, and AI-oriented search Document count and size, update rate, query mix, latency target, relevance tests, and vector dimensions

docs.title: Capacity profiles
docs.text:
Capacity Marketplace planning range Interpretation Small Up to 100 GB/day ingest and up to 2 TB stored Starting range for lighter workloads Medium 100–500 GB/day ingest and up to 10 TB stored Starting range for growing workloads Large At least 500 GB/day ingest and more than 10 TB stored Starting range for heavy workloads

These are planning ranges from the source definition, not performance, retention, cost, or service-level guarantees. Validate a representative workload before production.

docs.title: Topology choices
docs.text:
Topology Source-defined purpose Availability All-in-one A high-availability-ready layout without data tiering Search and Observability Master/data Dedicated master and data roles for balanced scale Search and Observability Master/hot/warm Dedicated masters with hot and warm data tiers Observability in the current source definition Optional ML Adds machine-learning capability when selected Requires deployment support and an eligible Elastic license

Node counts, Azure VM sizes, JVM heap, usable disk, replica policy, availability-zone placement, and horizontal scale increments are not published until the runtime configuration and live offer are verified.

docs.title: Require a versioned sizing record
docs.text:
Before approving a production profile, obtain a sizing record for the exact Marketplace plan and platform release. It must include:

Required value Why it matters Platform and Elastic versions Connects the sizing statement to a reproducible release Elasticsearch instance count and roles Establishes the physical topology behind the profile label AKS node-pool VM size and count Identifies the Azure compute consumed by the platform CPU, memory, and Elasticsearch JVM heap Supports workload and concurrency review Disk per instance and usable storage after replicas Prevents treating raw disk as customer-usable capacity Example daily ingest and retention assumptions Explains the workload model used for planning Baseline availability and placement Supports resilience and recovery review Horizontal scale increment Shows the operational effect of a capacity change Azure infrastructure-cost estimate and assumptions Supports commercial review in the customer's region Limits and excluded workloads Prevents unsupported use of a general size label

If the seller, approved offer, or service schedule does not provide these values, treat the physical sizing and cost as unresolved. The Small, Medium, and Large ranges alone are not enough for production approval.

docs.title: All-in-one
docs.text: All-in-one keeps Elasticsearch roles together. The three instances illustrate the source-defined minimum description, not a capacity guarantee.

docs.title: Dedicated master and data
docs.text: The master/data topology separates cluster coordination from data and query workloads.

docs.title: Dedicated master, hot, and warm
docs.text: The hot/warm topology separates active and historical data tiers. Lifecycle movement and retention still require an approved policy.

docs.title: Select a profile
docs.text:
1. Start with measured or estimated ingestion, retention, query, and user requirements.
  2. Review the resources and limitations displayed for each available choice.
  3. Confirm that the topology meets your availability requirements.
  4. Confirm that licensed features required by the workload are available.
  5. Validate the choice with representative ingest and query tests.
  6. Record the selected values and the evidence used for the decision.

docs.title: Plan scale and retention
docs.text:
Treat the selected capacity as a baseline, not a permanent ceiling. Record the profile's verified starting resources and supported scale-out increment for the exact platform release. Model retained storage after replicas, index overhead, and snapshots rather than using raw disk as searchable capacity.

Forecast daily ingestion, retention, shard growth, query concurrency, and data tiering together. Optional ML or AI capacity must be sized separately when the approved plan exposes it; enabling a feature does not prove that the selected resources meet workload demand.

docs.title: Avoid unsupported assumptions
docs.text:
• A size label is not a service-level objective.
  • Retention is not automatically implied by a topology.
  • Machine learning availability depends on both deployment configuration and the Elastic license.
  • A capacity change can affect cost, maintenance, and performance.

After deployment, monitor actual ingestion, shard count, disk use, query latency, and growth. Use health and capacity before requesting a profile change.

docs.title: Configure public access
docs.text: Use this procedure only when the deployment outputs identify public service URLs and your security policy permits public access.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Obtain from deployment details:

  • every public service hostname;
  • the authoritative DNS target or records requested by the deployment;
  • certificate status;
  • any approved source restrictions.

Do not invent an IP address or infer a target from an internal Azure resource.

docs.title: Configure public access and DNS
docs.text:
1. Ask the authoritative DNS owner to create exactly the records supplied by the deployment.
  2. Wait for the record's configured DNS time to live.

  3. From an approved client, query each hostname:

    nslookup <service-hostname>

  4. Confirm the answer matches the authoritative deployment target.

  5. Confirm that any deployment-supported source, proxy, or firewall restrictions match the approved access plan.

docs.title: Safe result
docs.text:
