DNS resolves consistently and TCP port 443 reaches the intended public endpoint. Complete TLS and application checks in verify access.

If the hostname does not resolve, verify the authoritative record. If it resolves but the connection fails, follow connectivity troubleshooting.

docs.text:
No platform version is listed until the product owner verifies:

  • the Marketplace offer and plan;
  • platform and Elastic versions;
  • supported regions and profiles;
  • managed actions and endpoints;
  • upgrade and compatibility boundaries;
  • release date and customer notification.

Each future platform entry must state the customer-visible changes, required actions, compatibility, security impact, known limitations, and support route.

Use compatibility to record the version of an existing deployment.

docs.title: Reset the administrator password
docs.text: Reset the initial administrator credential before onboarding users or data. Use only the credential-reset action exposed by the deployed managed application.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • a managed application that has reached platform readiness;
  • permission to run its customer-facing credential action;
  • an approved secrets system for the replacement password;
  • the Elasticsearch URL from deployment details for verification.

The action identifies the affected Elasticsearch administrator account. In deployments where it identifies the built-in elastic user, the new password applies to that account. Do not assume a username that the action does not display.

docs.title: Reset the credential
docs.text:
1. In the Azure portal, open Managed applications and select the deployed application.
  2. On the customer-facing application Overview or My Deployment view, open the available Elastic credential or administrator password-reset action.
  3. Confirm the displayed application and affected account before continuing.
  4. Generate or enter a unique password that meets the policy shown by the action.
  5. Save the password directly to the approved secrets system. Do not place it in a ticket, chat, screenshot, shell command, or documentation record.
  6. Submit the reset and wait until the action reports completion.

If no credential-reset action appears, do not modify a secret in the managed resource group. Use Contact support to confirm whether the action is available for the deployed plan and version.

docs.title: Verify the new credential
docs.text:
From an approved client with working DNS and TLS, run:

curl --fail-with-body --user "<administrator-user>" \
  "https://<elasticsearch-hostname>/"

Enter the new password when prompted. A valid credential returns the Elasticsearch product response; an HTTP authentication error means the reset, username, or credential entry must be checked.

Reserve the bootstrap administrator for recovery and tasks that require full cluster access. Continue with verify access, then create named least-privilege identities.

docs.title: Azure roles
docs.text:
The deploying user needs permission to create the managed application in the selected subscription and resource group. The application can also require role assignments for managed identities and supporting services.

Azure Contributor does not include permission to create every role assignment. Use the least-privilege role design approved by your Azure administrator rather than granting Owner by default.

Private Endpoint, VNet, private DNS, and DNS record changes may belong to different resource groups and teams. Assign only the resource-scoped roles needed for each task.

docs.title: Managed resource group
docs.text: Customer access can be limited by a deny assignment established by the managed application. Do not attempt to bypass it. Use supported managed actions or escalate.

docs.title: Elasticsearch and Kibana
docs.text:
Separate:

  • security administration;
  • cluster monitoring;
  • index ingestion;
  • index read access;
  • Kibana content creation;
  • Kibana read-only access.

Reserve the built-in elastic superuser for tasks that require unrestricted access. Use named users, SSO mappings, or scoped API keys for routine work.

Microsoft describes managed application permission boundaries in Azure Managed Applications overview.

docs.title: Search and visualize data
docs.text: Use Kibana after data is present in Elasticsearch and your user has access to the intended indices and Kibana space.

docs.title: Create a data view
docs.text:
1. Sign in to Kibana.
  2. Use the navigation search to open Data Views.
  3. Select Create data view.
  4. Enter an approved name and an index pattern that matches only the intended data.
  5. Select the timestamp field when the data has one.
  6. Save the data view.

If no matching indices appear, confirm that data has been indexed and that the current user has read access.

docs.title: Find events
docs.text:
1. Open Discover.
  2. Select the data view.
  3. Choose a time range that includes the indexed events.
  4. Filter by a known non-sensitive field.
  5. Add useful fields to the result table.
  6. Save the search only if other users need to reuse it.

docs.title: Create a first visualization
docs.text:
1. Open Dashboard and create a dashboard.
  2. Select Create visualization.
  3. Choose the data view and a simple count or time-series view.
  4. Verify that filters and time range affect the result as expected.
  5. Save the visualization and dashboard with descriptive names.

Use Kibana spaces and roles to separate teams. A missing result can be caused by an incorrect time range, data view, field, or permission. See Elastic search troubleshooting before changing index mappings or privileges.

docs.title: Verify access
docs.text: Run the checks from an approved customer network with the exact Elasticsearch and Kibana URLs from deployment details. Complete the checks in order so that an authentication symptom is not confused with a network, DNS, or TLS failure.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
• Complete the public or private network, DNS, and certificate tasks.
  • Reset the administrator password.
  • Keep credentials in an approved secrets system and enter them only through a protected client prompt or secret mechanism.

docs.title: Verify the access path
docs.text:
1. Resolve each service hostname:

    nslookup <service-hostname>

    Confirm the answer matches the authoritative public target or Private Endpoint recorded for this deployment.

  2. Test TCP and HTTPS reachability:

    nc -vz <service-hostname> 443

  3. Validate TLS with the exact hostname:

    SERVICE_HOSTNAME="<deployment-service-hostname>"

openssl s_client \
  -connect "${SERVICE_HOSTNAME}:443" \
  -servername "${SERVICE_HOSTNAME}" \
  -verify_return_error </dev/null

    Confirm the result is Verify return code: 0 (ok).

  4. Request the Elasticsearch root resource:

    curl --fail-with-body --user "<user>" \
  "https://<elasticsearch-hostname>/"

    Enter the password when prompted and confirm Elasticsearch returns its product response.

  5. Open the deployment-provided Kibana URL by hostname and confirm the sign-in page loads without a certificate or redirect error.

  6. Sign in with the approved credential and confirm Kibana loads for that identity.

docs.title: Optionally index a test document
docs.text:
Use a non-production test index and a user allowed to create, read, and delete only that index. Do not use production or sensitive data.

export ELASTICSEARCH_URL="https://<elasticsearch-hostname>"

curl --fail-with-body --user "<user>" \
  --request POST \
  "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/docs-validation/_doc?refresh=wait_for" \
  --header "Content-Type: application/json" \
  --data '{
    "@timestamp": "2026-08-12T00:00:00Z",
    "message": "documentation validation event",
    "environment": "test"
  }'

curl --fail-with-body --user "<user>" \
  "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/docs-validation/_search?q=environment:test"

curl --fail-with-body --user "<user>" \
  --request DELETE \
  "${ELASTICSEARCH_URL}/docs-validation"

Enter the password at each prompt. Confirm the document is returned by search and that deletion succeeds. Do not grant broad administrator access to bypass a test-index permission error.

docs.title: Finish setup
docs.text:
Create or map named least-privilege users and roles and reserve the bootstrap administrator for recovery or tasks that require full cluster access.

Your platform is ready to use. Continue by choosing a production data onboarding path.

docs.title: Shared responsibility
docs.text:
The managed application reduces infrastructure work, but it does not transfer ownership of your Azure subscription, identities, network, or data to iVedha.

The customer owns Azure and data decisions. iVedha and Opsflw manage the supported platform lifecycle without owning the customer's infrastructure.

docs.title: Responsibility overview
docs.text:
Area Customer iVedha Azure subscription, billing, policy, and quota Own and approve Identify deployment requirements Marketplace purchase and managed application Select, create, and delete Package and support the application Managed infrastructure Avoid unsupported changes Provision and operate supported components Network routes, peering, and client DNS Configure customer-side connectivity Provide authoritative deployment endpoints Private Endpoint Create in the client network Expose the deployment Private Link Service TLS Approve names and trust chain Apply supported certificate material Elasticsearch data and retention Classify, ingest, retain, and delete data Operate the managed platform Elasticsearch users and roles Assign least-privilege access Provide supported access mechanisms Snapshots and recovery objectives Define and test requirements Provide verified platform workflows Monitoring and support evidence Monitor workload outcomes and report symptoms Operate the managed-resource monitoring agent, receive its telemetry in the iVedha monitoring cluster, and investigate platform health

Microsoft operates Azure and enforces the Azure Managed Application and Marketplace contracts. Elastic defines Elasticsearch and Kibana product behavior, APIs, security features, and version compatibility.

The monitoring agent in the managed resource group forwards operational platform telemetry to the iVedha monitoring cluster for health monitoring and incident response. This monitoring flow does not transfer ownership of the customer's Azure resources, Elasticsearch indices, or application data to iVedha.

docs.title: Customer safety rules
docs.text:
• Do not edit, move, or delete resources in the managed resource group.
  • Do not reconstruct internal resource names from naming conventions.
  • Do not share passwords, private keys, access tokens, or unredacted diagnostics in tickets.
  • Obtain endpoint names and resource IDs from deployment details.
  • Test backups, access changes, and client configuration in a non-production environment when one is available.

Deleting the Azure managed application also deletes its managed resource group. Review delete the application before decommissioning.

docs.title: Configure single sign-on
docs.text: OIDC configuration is available only when the deployed managed application exposes an approved single-sign-on action. If the action is absent, do not change managed resources or Elasticsearch configuration directly; request an availability review.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
Coordinate with a Microsoft Entra application administrator and an Elasticsearch security administrator. Record:

  • tenant identity;
  • application client ID;
  • approved redirect URI shown by the deployment;
  • OpenID Connect metadata or issuer value required by the action;
  • claims used for user identity and group or role mapping;
  • groups and Elastic roles approved for the first test;
  • break-glass access and rollback owner.

Store the client secret in the secret mechanism required by the managed action. Do not put it in a deployment tag, wiki, screenshot, or ticket.

OpenID Connect supports interactive Kibana sign-in. It is not the authentication method for normal Elasticsearch REST clients. Keep a separate approved authentication method for API access and break-glass administration.

Microsoft Entra authenticates the user. Elasticsearch role mappings determine what the authenticated user can access.

docs.title: Register the application in Microsoft Entra
docs.text:
1. In the Microsoft Entra admin center, open App registrations.
  2. Create a single-tenant registration unless the approved service design explicitly requires another account type.
  3. Under Authentication, add a Web redirect URI.
  4. Copy the exact redirect URI from the managed application. Do not derive it from a hostname or example.
  5. Create the credential type required by the managed action and record its owner and expiration.
  6. Under Token configuration, configure only the approved claims.

The current managed-action source uses these defaults:

Managed field Default claim Purpose Claims Principal upn User identity supplied to the Elastic realm Claims Groups groups Group values available for role mapping Claims Name name Display name Claims Mail email Email attribute

Confirm the live action uses the same defaults. Microsoft Entra can omit the complete group list when a user belongs to many groups. Test a representative high-membership account and use an approved alternative mapping design when group overage occurs.

docs.title: Recognize the expected URI formats
docs.text:
Use the values exposed by the managed application. The following patterns help an Entra administrator recognize them; they are not substitutes for deployment-provided values.

Value Expected pattern Kibana callback ${KIBANA_URL}/api/security/oidc/callback for the authorization-code flow Entra issuer https://login.microsoftonline.com/${TENANT_ID}/v2.0 for a tenant-specific v2 endpoint Discovery document ${ENTRA_ISSUER}/.well-known/openid-configuration

The callback must use the externally visible Kibana URL and must match the Web redirect URI in Entra exactly, including scheme, host, path, port when present, and trailing-slash behavior. Do not reconstruct it when the managed application supplies a different value.

docs.title: Apply the managed OIDC configuration
docs.text:
1. Open the deployed managed application.
  2. Open Resources > My Deployment > Configure Deployment.
  3. Enable Change SSO OIDC Settings.
  4. Enter the verified client ID and credential through the protected password control.
  5. Confirm the principal, groups, name, email, and optional principal-pattern fields.
  6. Submit the change and wait for the managed action and synchronization to complete.

docs.title: Map users to Elastic roles
docs.text:
Authentication does not grant Elasticsearch privileges. Create least-privilege Elastic roles first, then map an approved Entra group or other stable claim to those roles through Kibana or the role-mapping API.

For example, a mapping rule can match one approved group identifier:

{
  "roles": ["kibana_reader"],
  "enabled": true,
  "rules": {
    "field": {
      "groups": "<approved-entra-group-object-id>"
    }
  },
  "metadata": {
    "owner": "identity-team"
  }
}

Replace the role and group with approved values. Do not map all authenticated users to a broad administrator role.

docs.title: Validate and recover
docs.text:
1. Test with a non-administrator account in a private browser session.
  2. Confirm the user receives only the intended Elasticsearch and Kibana privileges.
  3. Test a user with no mapped group and confirm access is denied or limited as designed.
  4. Test logout and a new session.
  5. Test the documented break-glass path before closing the change.
  6. Record the client credential's expiration and rotation owner.

Do not disable the last working administrative authentication method until OIDC sign-in and role mapping have been validated.

docs.title: Rotate the client credential
docs.text:
1. Confirm break-glass access works and schedule a supported configuration window.
  2. Create a second Entra credential before the current credential expires.
  3. Submit the new credential through Configure Deployment without deleting the working credential.
  4. Wait for managed synchronization to complete.
  5. Test sign-in and least-privilege role mapping in a private browser session.
  6. Remove the old Entra credential only after the new credential works.
  7. Record the new expiration, owner, and validation evidence.

Do not paste either credential into screenshots, browser developer tools, tickets, or documentation.

docs.title: Diagnose common sign-in failures
docs.text:
Symptom Check AADSTS50011 The callback sent by Kibana must exactly match a registered Entra Web redirect URI Invalid or expired client credential Confirm the managed action received the secret value, the credential is current, and synchronization completed Entra sign-in succeeds but Kibana denies access Confirm the principal or groups claim and the Elastic role mapping A high-membership user has no groups claim Check for Entra group-overage behavior and use an approved mapping alternative Redirect loop or immediate return to sign-in Check the issuer, callback, browser cookies, time synchronization, and managed realm status

Successful validation ends with Kibana loading for the test user and exposing only the spaces, indices, and actions assigned by the approved Elastic roles.

For a redirect mismatch, compare the value sent by Kibana with the Web redirect URI in Entra. For missing roles, inspect the identity and groups received by the Elastic realm without copying tokens into a ticket. Use Microsoft Entra OIDC guidance and Elastic OpenID Connect authentication for protocol and role-mapping behavior.

docs.title: Back up and restore
docs.text:
Elasticsearch snapshots store data and supported cluster state in an off-cluster repository. Azure storage access can be provisioned for snapshots, but do not assume that a repository, schedule, retention rule, or restore test is active until you verify it.

A restore is complete only after the customer validates recovered data, security, integrations, and application behavior.

docs.title: Verify backup readiness
docs.text:
1. In Kibana, use navigation search to open Snapshot and Restore.
  2. Confirm that the approved repository is registered and reachable.
  3. Review Snapshot Lifecycle Management policies.
  4. Confirm the last successful snapshot and its included data.
  5. Compare retention and frequency with the approved recovery objectives.
  6. Record the last restore-test date.

docs.title: Create an on-demand snapshot
docs.text: Before a high-risk change, create a snapshot through Kibana or the approved Elasticsearch API. Give it a descriptive, non-sensitive name. Wait for success and confirm that failed or partial shards are not being overlooked.

docs.title: Plan a restore
docs.text:
1. Identify the exact snapshot and indices or feature state to restore.
  2. Review version compatibility and name conflicts.
  3. Confirm the required cluster and repository privileges.
  4. Define the effect on current data, writes, aliases, and clients.
  5. Obtain change approval and a maintenance window.
  6. Restore into a non-production target first when possible.
  7. Validate document counts, searches, Kibana objects, permissions, and application behavior.

Snapshots are not copies of Azure managed infrastructure. Coordinate a full-service recovery with iVedha.

See Elastic snapshot and restore for product behavior and compatibility requirements.

docs.title: Troubleshoot connectivity problems
docs.text: Run tests from an affected client and, when possible, a known-good client. Start with the shared sequence in Start troubleshooting here.

docs.title: 1. Check the endpoint
docs.text:
For private access, confirm:

  • the Private Endpoint exists;
  • its connection status is Approved;
  • the private IP has not changed;
  • the client has a route to its subnet;
  • network security controls permit the connection.

Test TCP connectivity without sending credentials:

nc -vz <service-hostname> 443

docs.title: 2. Check DNS
docs.text:
nslookup <service-hostname>

For private access, the result must be the Private Endpoint private IP. If the result is NXDOMAIN, public, or stale, check the private zone, records, VNet links, custom DNS, and conditional forwarding.

Microsoft documents common causes in Private Endpoint DNS resolution.

docs.title: 3. Check TLS
docs.text:
SERVICE_HOSTNAME="<deployment-service-hostname>"

openssl s_client \
  -connect "${SERVICE_HOSTNAME}:443" \
  -servername "${SERVICE_HOSTNAME}" \
  -verify_return_error </dev/null

Check certificate dates, subject alternative names, intermediate certificates, and client trust. A successful check ends with Verify return code: 0 (ok).

Common results:

Result Investigate Name or service not known DNS name, resolver, private zone, or forwarding Timeout or refused connection Route, firewall, Private Endpoint, endpoint health, or port unable to get local issuer certificate Missing intermediate or client trust anchor Hostname mismatch Wrong DNS name or certificate subject alternative name Expired certificate Certificate renewal and managed action status

Do not disable certificate verification as a fix.

docs.title: 4. Check authentication
docs.text:
Only after TLS works, confirm the account is active and has the intended roles. Test in a private browser session to exclude stale cookies.

If the same failure remains after these checks, get support with redacted results.

docs.title: Troubleshoot deployment problems
docs.text: Complete the safe first-response checks in Start troubleshooting here before changing a deployment input or escalating.

docs.title: Azure validation fails before creation
docs.text:
1. Read the complete validation message.
  2. Confirm the selected subscription, region, and application resource group.
  3. Check Marketplace purchase policy and plan availability.
  4. Check Azure Policy denials, registered resource providers, and quota.
  5. Check whether the deploying identity may create required role assignments.
  6. Correct the approved input and rerun Review + create.

Do not bypass policy or grant Owner merely to test a hypothesis.

docs.title: An ARM deployment fails
docs.text:
1. Open the application resource group.
  2. Open Deployments and select the failed operation.
  3. Record the deployment name, time, correlation ID, error code, and redacted error message.
  4. Identify the first failed operation rather than only the final cascade.
  5. Check for policy, quota, name, region, RBAC, or network conflicts.
  6. Do not delete or edit partially created resources unless the managed application procedure instructs you to do so.

docs.title: Azure succeeds but the service is not ready
docs.text:
1. Confirm that the managed application still exists and reports success.
  2. Review deployment outputs for endpoints and status.
  3. Check whether the managed application exposes a readiness or synchronization state.
  4. Wait while progress is changing.
  5. Escalate when progress stops, required outputs never appear, or the service remains unavailable.

Include safe deployment evidence when you get support.

docs.title: Troubleshoot Elasticsearch problems
docs.text: Use a user with only the diagnostic privileges required for the affected operation. Complete the endpoint, DNS, TLS, and authentication checks in Start troubleshooting here first.

docs.title: Check cluster health
docs.text:
curl --fail-with-body --user "<user>" \
  "https://<elasticsearch-hostname>/_cluster/health?pretty"

Record status, unassigned shards, node count, and task symptoms.

docs.title: Writes are blocked or return HTTP 429
docs.text: Check disk use and watermark messages. At flood stage, Elasticsearch can mark affected indices read-only. Reduce avoidable ingestion, remove data only under an approved retention decision, or request supported capacity. Do not permanently raise watermarks to mask a full disk.

docs.title: Search returns no results
docs.text:
1. Confirm the index or data stream contains documents.
  2. Confirm the user can read it.
  3. Check the Kibana data view and time range.
  4. Confirm the expected field exists and has the intended type.
  5. Check whether data was written to another index or pipeline.

docs.title: Kibana is not ready
docs.text: Confirm Elasticsearch connectivity and health first. Disk pressure, unavailable system indices, authentication, or certificate failures can prevent Kibana from becoming ready.

docs.title: Ingest fails
docs.text:
Record the status code and redacted error type. Check mapping conflicts, pipeline errors, rejected requests, permissions, and target index names. Test a synthetic document rather than replaying sensitive production data.

Use Elastic troubleshooting for current product diagnostics, then get support if the managed service requires intervention.

docs.title: Start troubleshooting here
docs.text: Begin with the user-visible symptom and stop at the first failing layer. Do not edit managed resources, disable TLS verification, or broaden privileges while testing a hypothesis.

docs.title: First-response sequence
docs.text:
1. Identify the affected component. Record whether the symptom affects the Azure deployment, endpoint path, Elasticsearch, Kibana, ingestion, or one user.
  2. Check platform readiness. Confirm Azure deployment state, managed application health, synchronization, and published endpoints.
  3. Check the endpoint. For private access, confirm the Private Endpoint is approved and the client has a route. For public access, confirm the deployment-supported path is allowed.
  4. Check DNS. Resolve the exact service hostname from an affected client and compare it with deployment details.
  5. Check TLS. Validate certificate dates, SANs, chain, and client trust without disabling verification.
  6. Check authentication. Confirm the account or key is current and test only after DNS and TLS work.
  7. Check Elasticsearch and Kibana health. Review cluster health, capacity, blocked writes, service readiness, and the specific failing operation.
  8. Collect evidence. Record timestamps, impact, safe identifiers, correlation IDs, status codes, and redacted errors.
  9. Escalate when required. Use the managed application's support route when the failing layer requires iVedha action or the safe checks do not isolate the cause.

docs.title: Choose the issue guide
docs.text:
Symptom Continue with Marketplace validation, ARM failure, stalled reconciliation, or missing outputs Deployment issues Private Endpoint, route, DNS, TLS, browser, or connection failure Connectivity issues Unhealthy cluster, blocked writes, missing search results, ingest failure, or Kibana not ready Elasticsearch issues Managed intervention or escalation is required Contact support

Use a known-good client for comparison when available. Keep customer data, credentials, tokens, private keys, cookies, and unredacted deployment parameters out of diagnostics and tickets.

docs.title: Prepare for upgrades
docs.text: Do not upgrade Elasticsearch, Kibana, Kubernetes, or managed infrastructure directly. Use only a version or maintenance action approved for the managed application.

docs.title: Prepare
docs.text:
1. Record the current Elasticsearch and Kibana versions.
  2. Review Elastic breaking changes and deprecations for the complete upgrade path.
  3. Check client, integration, plugin, and ingest-component compatibility.
  4. Resolve critical cluster-health and disk-capacity problems.
  5. Verify a recent successful snapshot and the restore plan.
  6. Pause unrelated configuration changes.
  7. Define validation, rollback, owners, and customer communications.

Elasticsearch does not support downgrading to an earlier version. Treat rollback as a service recovery decision, not as an ordinary package downgrade.

docs.title: Validate after the managed upgrade
docs.text:
• Confirm the reported Elasticsearch and Kibana versions.
  • Check cluster health and unassigned shards.
  • Test authentication and role mappings.
  • Test one representative indexing and search operation.
  • Open critical Kibana dashboards.
  • Confirm ingestion clients and snapshot policies are healthy.
  • Review deprecation or migration warnings.

Use Elastic upgrade preparation for current compatibility requirements. If no managed upgrade action is available, get support rather than changing infrastructure.

docs.title: Manage users and roles
docs.text: Use named identities and least-privilege roles. Do not use the built-in elastic superuser for routine ingestion, dashboards, or read-only access.

docs.title: Design access
docs.text:
For each persona, identify:

  • required indices or data streams;
  • read, write, create, delete, or lifecycle operations;
  • required Kibana spaces and features;
  • any cluster-level operation;
  • access owner and review date.

Separate data ingestion, data exploration, content administration, and cluster administration roles.

docs.title: Create and test a role
docs.text:
1. Sign in to Kibana with an authorized security administrator.
  2. Open Roles using Kibana navigation search.
  3. Create a role with only the required cluster, index, and Kibana privileges.
  4. Restrict index patterns and Kibana spaces.
  5. Save the role.
  6. Create or select a named user and assign the role.
  7. Sign in with a test identity and verify both permitted and denied actions.
  8. Record the owner and review date outside the password or token store.

docs.title: Protect credentials
docs.text:
• Store service credentials and API keys in an approved secret manager.
  • Prefer short-lived or scoped credentials.
  • Rotate credentials when ownership changes or exposure is suspected.
  • Never include authentication headers, passwords, or API keys in tickets.
  • Disable unused accounts rather than sharing them.

For product behavior, see Elastic user authentication.
